common_name: Bluegem Rabbiteye Blueberry (Historic Low-Chill Florida Selection)

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in acidic, well-drained, organic-matter-rich soil; Bluegem carries one of the lowest chill requirements among rabbiteye selections, historically valued for reliable bud break even after Gulf South winters too mild for most other rabbiteye cultivars.

directions: Set dormant plants into raised, sulfur-amended beds if the native soil isn't already strongly acidic, and mulch heavily with pine bark to buffer root temperatures through long Gulf Coast summers. Bluegem was among the earliest named rabbiteye selections released by University of Florida breeders in the 1950s, prized for setting a full fruit crop even in unusually warm, low-chill winters that leave many later rabbiteye cultivars with erratic bloom. The medium, light-blue berries have a firm skin and mild flavor, ripening over a fairly long midseason window. Plant it alongside a second rabbiteye cultivar such as Climax or Brightwell for cross-pollination, and renewal-prune the oldest canes out each winter to keep the bush productive.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Blueberry Gardener's Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in winter into very acidic, well-drained soil; Ethel is one of the original Georgia Coastal Plain rabbiteye releases from the same 1950s breeding effort that produced Homebell and Menditoo, and needs another rabbiteye cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Amend planting beds to a strongly acidic pH before setting out dormant plants, and mulch with pine straw or pine bark to keep the shallow, fibrous root system cool and moist. Ethel is a foundational rabbiteye selection released by the Georgia Coastal Plain Experiment Station in the 1950s, part of the same breeding cohort as Homebell, Menditoo, and Callaway, though it has been largely superseded commercially by later, higher-yielding cultivars like Tifblue and Climax. It still produces vigorous, disease-tolerant bushes with medium-sized, mild-flavored berries and is grown today mainly by heritage-variety collectors and small Southern homesteads. Prune out the oldest wood each winter and plant with a compatible rabbiteye pollinator for a full fruit set.

common_name: Black Giant Rabbiteye Blueberry (Historic Large-Fruited Georgia Selection)

planting.note: Plant during dormancy in acidic, well-drained soil; Black Giant is a historic Georgia rabbiteye release named for its unusually large, dark berries, and requires a second rabbiteye cultivar nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant dormant bushes into raised, well-drained beds amended to a strongly acidic pH, spacing generously since this cultivar builds an especially large, spreading frame over time. Black Giant dates to the same mid-20th-century Georgia rabbiteye breeding program that produced Homebell and Ethel, and it earned its name from unusually large, deep-blue-black berries with a firm skin that holds up well to handling. It is a vigorous, long-lived bush but ripens its crop somewhat unevenly compared to modern cultivars, so home growers should expect to pick over several weeks rather than in one concentrated flush. Keep it mulched with pine bark and prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to maintain fruit quality.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in winter into acidic, well-drained soil; Coastal is a mid-20th-century Georgia rabbiteye release from the same Tifton breeding program as Homebell and Menditoo, best suited to home orchards wanting a genetically diverse pollinator partner.

directions: Set out dormant plants in winter into sulfur-amended, well-drained beds, and mulch with pine bark to conserve moisture through hot Gulf South summers. Coastal is one of the original named rabbiteye releases from the Georgia Coastal Plain Experiment Station's 1950s breeding program, sharing parentage with Homebell and Menditoo, both already grown across the Deep South. Its medium blue berries have a pleasant, mild flavor, and the bush itself is notably heat- and drought-tolerant once established, reflecting its native Coastal Plain selection. Because it is not self-fruitful, interplant with another rabbiteye cultivar and prune out the oldest canes each winter to sustain vigorous new growth.

common_name: Cardinal Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early-Season NC State Release)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in winter into very acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark; Cardinal is an NC State University highbush release with a moderate chill requirement, best suited to the upper Gulf South rather than the mildest coastal zones.

directions: Plant into raised beds of very acidic, well-drained soil and mulch thickly with pine bark to protect the fibrous, shallow root system. Cardinal is an early-ripening southern highbush cultivar released by North Carolina State University, valued for producing a concentrated flush of firm, light-blue, well-flavored berries near the start of the harvest season, ahead of most rabbiteye cultivars. Because its chill requirement runs a bit higher than true low-chill Florida-bred selections, it performs best in the cooler, more inland parts of zone 9a rather than immediately along the Gulf. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and after harvest, and prune out the oldest wood each winter to keep new fruiting canes coming.

common_name: Blue Ridge Southern Highbush Blueberry (Large-Fruited NC State Release)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes during winter into very acidic, well-drained soil; Blue Ridge is an NC State southern highbush release bred for large fruit size and good flavor, with a moderate chill requirement that favors the cooler margins of the Gulf South.

directions: Establish dormant, container-grown plants in winter in raised, acid-amended beds, keeping the shallow root zone mulched with pine bark year-round. Blue Ridge is a North Carolina State University southern highbush release bred primarily for large berry size and rich flavor rather than for the very lowest chill requirements, so it rewards growers in the cooler, more inland pockets of the Gulf South with fewer, larger-scale flushes of fruit than the deep-South low-chill cultivars. The upright, vigorous bush holds fruit well without excessive splitting during summer rains. Renewal-prune the oldest canes each winter and pair it with another midseason highbush cultivar to extend the harvest window.

common_name: Peach Sorbet Dwarf Blueberry (Compact Container Blueberry with Colorful Foliage)

planting.note: Plant year-round from containers in mild Gulf Coast winters, or during dormancy elsewhere, into acidic, well-drained potting mix or raised beds; Peach Sorbet is a compact patented selection from Fall Creek Farm & Nursery's Bushel and Berry collection, bred with a low enough chill requirement to fruit reliably in warm Southern gardens and patio containers.

directions: Grow Peach Sorbet in a large container or raised bed filled with an acidic, well-drained azalea-and-camellia mix, since its compact, mounding habit makes it as much a landscape or patio accent as a fruiting shrub. New spring foliage emerges a soft peachy-pink before turning green for summer, then shifts back to shades of orange and purple as nights cool in fall, giving three seasons of color in addition to the berries. Being self-fertile, a single plant will set fruit, though yields improve with a second nearby blueberry for cross-pollination. Water deeply and regularly since containers dry out faster than garden beds, and top-dress with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring.

common_name: Pink Icing Dwarf Blueberry (Compact Container Blueberry with Blue-and-Pink Foliage)

planting.note: Plant from containers into acidic, well-drained potting mix or raised beds; Pink Icing is a compact, low-chill Bushel and Berry selection bred by Fall Creek Farm & Nursery for ornamental foliage color as much as fruit, and performs well in warm-winter Gulf South gardens.

directions: Site Pink Icing in a container or small raised bed of acidic, well-drained soil where its blue-green summer foliage and pink-to-purple fall color can be appreciated up close near a patio or entryway. The compact, rounded habit stays small enough for tight garden spaces yet still produces a respectable crop of sweet, powder-blue berries in early to midsummer on a self-fertile plant. Because container-grown blueberries dry out quickly in Gulf Coast heat, check soil moisture often and never let the root ball go bone-dry. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and refresh the potting mix every couple of years as it breaks down.

common_name: Jelly Bean Dwarf Blueberry (Cold-Hardy Compact Container Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant from containers into acidic, well-drained potting mix or raised beds; Jelly Bean is a compact Bushel and Berry selection from Fall Creek Farm & Nursery bred for an unusually wide climate range, fruiting acceptably in both cold-winter and mild Southern gardens.

directions: Grow Jelly Bean in a container or compact raised bed filled with acidic, well-drained soil, taking advantage of its dense, tidy, rounded form for small-space edible landscaping. It is one of the more broadly climate-adaptable selections in the dwarf Bushel and Berry line, tolerating both colder winters and the mild, low-chill winters typical of the Gulf South, though fruit set in the warmest zones benefits from siting where it gets full winter sun exposure. Sweet, marble-sized berries ripen over several weeks in early summer on a self-fertile plant, though a second blueberry nearby improves yield. Keep the potting mix consistently moist and top-dress with acid-forming fertilizer each spring.

common_name: Perpetua Everbearing Dwarf Blueberry (Reblooming Two-Harvest Container Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant from containers into acidic, well-drained potting mix or raised beds; Perpetua is a compact, everbearing Bushel and Berry selection from Fall Creek Farm & Nursery that produces a second late-summer to fall flush of fruit in addition to the normal early-summer crop, an unusual trait for a blueberry.

directions: Give Perpetua a large container or raised bed of acidic, well-drained soil, since it grows a bit larger than the other dwarf Bushel and Berry selections while still staying compact enough for a patio or small yard. What sets it apart is a genuine second bloom and fruit set in late summer, so gardeners get an early-summer crop followed weeks later by a smaller fall harvest, on a self-fertile plant. This reblooming habit makes it especially useful in a mild Gulf Coast climate where the growing season is long enough to ripen both flushes before frost. Deadhead spent fruit clusters after the first harvest to encourage the second bloom, and feed with acid-forming fertilizer after each fruiting cycle.
